items.name: United Kingdom
items.history:
The United Kingdom declared war on Nazi Germany on 3 September 1939, after the German invasion of Poland. After the defeat of France in the spring of 1940, the British Expeditionary Force withdrew from the European Continent. Although the Channel Islands near the French coast did fall into German hands, from the summer of 1940 until 1945, mainland Britain resisted German invasion and became a refuge for many governments-in-exile and refugees of the occupied countries in Europe.

At the outbreak of the war, 370,000 to 390,000 Jews were living in the UK, out of a total population of about 48 million. The Channel Islands were home to only a few dozen Jews. Anti-Jewish measures on the Islands were issued by the German military authorities in Paris and followed the timing of those in France. They were implemented by the German military administration with the assistance of local authorities. In both Guernsey and Jersey, antisemitic legislation was passed by the Royal Court. About ten Jews were deported. The Nazis operated a number of concentration and forced labour camps on the island of Alderney from January 1942 with approximately 5,000, mostly Eastern European inmates. About 890 of the prisoners were French Jewish forced labourers, at least 8 of whom died there. The United Kingdom had begun accepting refugees following the November Pogrom of 1938 when the British Government agreed to allow an unrestricted number of unaccompanied Jewish children to enter the country, a measure which remained in effect until the war broke out in September 1939. In total, approximately 65,000 Jewish refugees found shelter in the UK. British forces liberated concentration camps in northern Germany, including Neuengamme and Bergen-Belsen. 

At the outbreak of the Second World War, there were an estimated 45,000 Roma in England, which was the majority of Roma in the United Kingdom. Despite existing prejudices, Roma contributed to the war effort against Nazi Germany in manifold ways. The UK was an important country for gathering information on what was happening to Roma in German-occupied and -dominated Europe during and after the Second World War.
items.situation:
As the official archive for the UK Government, The National Archives in London houses records from the UK central government and central courts. The Public Records Act (1958) places responsibility for the management of public records on departments. Additional repositories also exist on Jersey and Guernsey. In addition to The National Archives, the UK is home to a number of independent and affiliated archives, such as The Wiener Holocaust Library; the Island Archives in Guernsey; the Jersey Archives; the Imperial War Museums; the Polish Institute and Sikorski Museum; and the Polish Underground Movement Study Trust. For more information on these institutions, see below.

With regard to archives related to Romani communities, the University of Leeds holds the “Gypsy, Traveller and Roma Collection”, including the Donald Kenrick collection. The Wiener Holocaust Library also holds some of the Kenrick collection as well as photographs and eyewitness accounts. The Roma Support Group holds oral histories, some of which relate to intergenerational impacts of genocide.
items.summary: [Test update] EHRI has merged and updated the existing information about archives holding Holocaust-relevant materials in the UK. The portal contains over twenty repositories holding Holocaust-related materials in the UK, including The National Archives, the Island Archives in Guernsey, the Jersey Archives and the Imperial War Museums in London. The Polish Institute and Sikorski Museum as well as the Polish Underground Movement Study Trust hold important Holocaust-related material generated by the Polish government-in-exile as well as the Polish underground in occupied Poland. The Wiener Holocaust Library is the oldest Holocaust memorial institution in the world. Founded as the Jewish Central Information Office in 1933 by Dr Alfred Wiener, the Library has been based in London since 1939, and holds extensive collections including published and unpublished works, eyewitness accounts, photographs and press cuttings. An important task of the EHRI project in the UK was to include information about the collections held by the Wiener Library in the EHRI Portal. Most of the Wiener Library collections have descriptions written by a member of the Wiener Library archive staff. These collection descriptions are included in the Archives Hub and the export of these descriptions from this Archives Hub to the EHRI Portal has been completed.
items.extensive:
Disclaimer: The EHRI Extensive Report was updated in 2024.

**A. EHRI approach to the United Kingdom: Pre-existing research, archival guides, and expert support**

In the United Kingdom, EHRI has identified, with the support of EHRI partner Wiener Library, a number of online research tools and traditional archival guides:

- [AIM25](http://www.aim25.ac.uk/)

AIM25 is a major project that provides electronic access to collection level descriptions of archives from over one hundred higher education institutions, learned societies, cultural organisations and City livery companies within the greater London area. This work is in progress – new data is being added regularly. EHRI partner Wiener Library is participating in this project.

- [The Archives Hub](http://www.archiveshub.ac.uk/)

The Archives Hub is a service funded by the Joint Information Systems Committee. It provides access to descriptions of archival collections held across the UK. At present it covers the descriptions of approximately 200 collection holding institutions. EHRI partner Wiener Library is participating in this project.

- [Yerusha Portal](https://yerusha.eu/)

The Yerusha portal, which incorporates Jewish-related archives around the world and ingests some of the WL’s collections, as well as Southampton, LmA, etc. might be useful to include. Aggregates Jewish archives, not solely focused on the Holocaust

Among the traditional archival guides, the following should be mentioned:
- [2000] Wilkinson, Mary & Julie Robertshaw, *Select catalogue of English-language material on the Holocaust held in the department of printed books* (London: Imperial War Museum, Department of Printed Books, 2000),
- [1993] Cantwell, John D., *The Second World War. A guide to documents in the Public Record Office* (London: HMSO, 1993).

An important task of the EHRI project in the UK was to include information about the collections held by the Wiener Holocaust Library in the EHRI Portal. Most of the Wiener Holocaust Library collections have descriptions written by the library’s staff. These collection descriptions are included in the Archives Hub mentioned above and have been exported from here to the EHRI Portal.

**B. Characteristics of the British archival system and specific challenges**

The National Archives in London are the official archives for the UK Government, storing its records and those of the United Kingdom’s central courts. The Public Records Act (1958) places responsibility for the management of public records on departments. Additional repositories of The National Archives also exist on the Channel Islands, Jersey and Guernsey. In addition to The National archives, there are many private archive initiatives.

**C. EHRI identification and description results on the United Kingdom**

**C.I. In the United Kingdom**

In the United Kingdom, EHRI has identified over 20 repositories, and is able to provide over hundreds of archival descriptions from several institutions. The Wiener Holocaust Library is the oldest Holocaust memorial institution in the world. Founded as the Jewish Central Information Office in 1933 by Dr Alfred Wiener, the Library has been based in London since 1939 and holds extensive collections including published and unpublished works, eyewitness accounts, photographs and press cuttings.

Holocaust-related material, however, is held by many other archival institutions, such as the Island Archives in Guernsey, which hold extensive collections on the German occupation of Guernsey (1940-1945), including those of the Feldkommandantur and the local civil administration, or Jersey Archives, which stores registration cards and significant records of all aspects from the German occupation. In The National Archives, there are very important documents relating to the Second World War and the Holocaust among the British government and military records. The most popular are within departments War Office (WO), Home Office (HO), Prime Minister’s Office Records (PREM) and Foreign Office (FO). The National Archives also holds records of war crimes and criminals (both alleged and proved) from 1939–1945 as well as copies of documents captured by the Western Allied forces from enemy powers at the end of the Second World War. Furthermore, the Imperial War Museum in London has collections ranging from film and oral history to works of art and large objects, but also to personal letters and diaries. The Polish Institute and Sikorski Museum as well as the Polish Underground Movement Study Trust hold important Holocaust-related material generated by the Polish government-in-exile as well as the Polish underground in occupied Poland. The collections in the Sikorski Institute are now regarded as holding the most important Polish émigré collections in the world. An extensive description of the Institute and its holdings can be found in Alina Skibińska’s archival guide, which has been revised and translated into English as part of EHRI’s efforts to make Holocaust-relevant sources linked to Poland easier to locate.

Finally, archives in the UK also house many sources about the Holocaust in other countries, mainly concerning British intelligence on what was happening in occupied Europe as well as the reactions of the governments-in-exile and resistance movements located in the UK.

**C.II. In other countries**

Outside of the United Kingdom, the United State Memorial Museum, Yad Vashem hold collections that are relevant to Holocaust research on the United Kingdom.
